newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hopes dashed for bumper S.African 1997 maize crop.
newsitem.headline: Hopes dashed for bumper S.African 1997 maize crop.

text.p: South Africa's maize crop will be almost two million tonnes smaller than last season, scotching hopes of another bumper harvest and strong export earnings for the country, latest official estimates show.
Output could be driven lower still if the widespread rains seen in recent weeks did not continue, industry experts said on Thursday.
Releasing its first official crop estimate the National Crop Estimates Committee said on Thursday it expected a new crop of 7.564 million tonnes, sharply down from 9.484 million in 1996.

The crop, which will be harvested from May, was expected to deliver 4.002 million tonnes of white maize and 3.562 million tonnes of yellow. This compared with 5.440 million tonnes of white and 4.044 million tonnes of yellow last year.
Kobus Smit, chairman of the crop committee, said dry weather in the major maize-growing areas of the North West province and western Free State was the culprit behind the fall.
"The lower crop boils down to the mere fact that we have had less rain," he told Reuters.
"The crop is a little above average and it is a bit more than average consumption which is between six and 6-1/2 million tonnes," he said.

Asked if there was scope for an increase in the estimate, which is revised monthly, he said: "No, it should not go up...If the rains continue like this for another month or so it should be maintained."
The U.S. Department of Agriculture earlier this month slashed its estimate of South Africa's harvest by one million tonnes to 8.5 million.

Kit le Clus, a director at the National Maize Producers Organisation, said that with the crop approaching a balance between supply and demand, the industry should finish its procurement as soon as possible.
"We advise farmers and consumers to urgently contract forward with one another to prevent the exports of further maize. There has been some maize contracted for exports already," le Clus said.

South Africa's maize market will be completely deregulated for the first time from the start of the new season on May 1, leaving private traders free to export as much product as they want. In the current season, government still set export limits.
Rod Blondin, the general manager of the South African Futures Exchange on which maize contracts are traded, said the smaller crop may force prices higher.
"To a certain extent it has been discounted in the market, we saw prices soaring a few weeks ago. But we could well see a further push in futures prices," Blondin said.
On Thursday white maize contracts for July delivery were being bid at 617 rand and offered at 619 after touching a high of 690 rand in February when dry conditions were at their most severe.
July yellow maize was bid at 590 and offered at 605 from a 670 rand high.
Le Clus said realistic prices on the physical market currently ranged between 550 and 600 rand a tonne, net to the farmer depending on the locality.
